cover_hook: Moth swarms are back after a 99.5% crash
caption_hook: 🦋 Australia's Bogong moths lost 99.5% of their numbers. Now swarms are filling the night sky again + 3 more wins 👇
question: Describe this comeback in one emoji 👇
share_line: Send this to someone who needs a comeback story
reel_hook: 99.5% of these moths vanished. They're back
first_comment: Bonus: these moths navigate by the Milky Way. In 2025 they became the first invertebrates shown to use the stars for such long trips. Did you know insects could read the sky?

stories.headline: Moth swarms that once blocked out the stars are back
stories.summary: Drought, pesticides and habitat loss wiped out an estimated 99.5% of Australia's Bogong moths after 2017. This spring, scientists are seeing big migrating swarms again, likely helped by wetter weather.
stories.why: The moths pollinate plants and feed the critically endangered mountain pygmy possum.

stories.headline: A new stick insect lays eggs with tiny lids
stories.summary: University of Sydney scientists found 2 new giant stick insect species. One, from the endangered Mabi rainforest, lays eggs with a lid-like structure never recorded in any stick insect before.
stories.why: Even Australia's most photographed insects still hide species nobody had named.

stories.headline: Crew-13 makes the fastest US trip ever to the space station
stories.summary: SpaceX's Dragon reached the ISS just 7 hours 55 minutes after launch, a US record. The last crew took over 30 hours. Commander Jessica Watkins is the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit.
stories.why: Faster trips mean less time cramped in a capsule, and a historic first for the crew.

stories.stat_label: storeys its walls could have held
stories.headline: A 2,800-year-old palace was built like a skyscraper
stories.summary: Computer models of the Grat Be'al Gibri palace in Ethiopia show its timber-laced stone walls could have carried about 16 storeys, double the 8 floors archaeologists had imagined.
stories.why: It shows how advanced builders in the Horn of Africa were nearly 3,000 years ago.

fun_fact: Bogong moth swarms once confused forecasters at the Sydney 2000 Olympics, who mistook them for rain on radar.
